lines.text: אור 27 אז
Zend and Sanscr. vara, fortification,
comp. Sanscr. pura a fortified city, after
the analogy of punar, Pracrit. unar, etc.
See F. Benary in the Berliner Jahrbb.
אוֹרָה f. 1. light, Ps. 139, 12; metaph.
of welfare, happiness, Esth. 8, 16.
2. Plur. אוֹרוֹת greens, green herbs, 2 K.
4, 39. The idea of brightness, splendour,
is often transferred in the Semitic
tongues to verdure and flowers; comp.
נִצִּץ, Arab. انوار lights and flowers.
Comp. also Samarit. יאר Gen. 1, 11. 12,
for דֶּשֶׁא herb.—So Is. 26, 19 כִּי טַל אוֹרוֹת
טַלֶּךָ for as the dew of herbs is thy dew,
i. e. God’s quickening influence will raise
the dead to life, as the dew of heaven
refreshes plants. Comp. Ecclus. 46, 12.
49, 10. Others render dew of light, i. e.
of life, the vivifying dew, comp. אוֹר d.
אֲוֵרוֹת by transp. for אֻרָיוֹת q. v. stalls,
cribs, 2 Chr. 32, 28.
אוּרִי (fiery, or perh. an abridged form
for אוּרִיָּה) Uri, pr. n. m. a) Ex. 31, 2.
אוּרִיאֵל (flame of God) Uriel, pr. n. m.
אוּרִיָּה (flame of Jehovah) Uriah, pr.
n. m. a) A Hittite, the husband of Bath-
sheba, treacherously slain by order of
David, 2 Sam. 11, 3. b) A priest in the
time of Ahaz and Isaiah, Is. 8, 2. 2 K.
אוּרִיָּהוּ (id.) Urijah, pr. n. of a prophet
slain by order of Jehoiakim, Jer. 26, 20 sq.
אוּשׁ see הִתְאוֹשֵׁשׁ under אִישׁ.
* אוֹת or אוּת a root not used in Kal.
Niph. נֵאוֹת, fut. 1 plur. נֵאוֹת, 3 plur.
יֵאוֹתוּ, to consent, 2 K. 12, 9; with dat. of
pers. to consent unto any one, to gratify
him, Gen. 34, 15. 22. 23. In Arabic this
sense is found under the form أَتَى i. q.
אָתָה to come, Conj. III اأَتَى, Heb. אוֹתָה,
whence seems to have arisen the new
root אוֹה; unless by changing the points,
instead of נֵאוֹת, יֵאֹתוּ, we prefer to read
נֵאוֹת, יֵאוֹתוּ, which forms may then be
referred to Poel of r. אָתָה.
I. אוֹת, plur. אֹתוֹת, comm. gend. comp.
sing. Gen. 9, 12. Ex. 4, 8; plur. Ex. 4, 9.
Josh. 24, 17. Contr. for אֹוֶת from אָוָה III,
comp. أَيَةٌ or آيَةٌ sign, for أَوِيَةٌ from
اوى.
1. a sign, Chald. אָת; Syr. ܐܳܬܳܐ, plur.
וְהָיוּ לְאֹתֹת וּלְמוֹעֲדִים and they shall be
for signs and for seasons, i. e. by Hen-
diadys, for signs of seasons.—Then
2. an ensign, flag, military standard,
espec. of each single tribe, Num. 2, 2 sq.
different from דֶּגֶל the banner of three
tribes together.
3. a sign of something past, a token,
memorial, Ex. 13, 9. 16. Deut. 6, 8.
Hence a memorial, monument, Is. 55, 13.
4. a sign of something future, a por-
tent, omen, τύπος τοῦ μέλλοντος Rom. 5,
14, i. q. מוֹפֵת. Is. 8, 18 lo! I and the
children whom Jehovah hath given me
are signs and portents in Israel from the
Lord of hosts, i. e. through the names
divinely given us, which are all of good
omen, (viz. יְשַׁעְיָה salvation of Jehovah;
עִמָּנוּאֵל God with us, 7, 14. 8, 8; Shear-
Jashub 7, 3,) God has made us types of
future things to prefigure future deliver-
ance and prosperity. Comp. 20, 3. Ez.
5. a sign or token of any thing in itself
not visible or discernible; e. g. the token
of a covenant, as circumcision, Gen. 17,
11; the sabbath, Ex. 31, 13. Hence
a token, argument, proof, Job 21, 29;
comp. Lat. signum Cic. de Invent. 1. 34,
Gr. τεκμήριον, σημεῖον, Sept. Job 21, 29.
So of the prophetic sign or token of the
truth of a prophecy, viz. when God or
the prophet as his interpreter foretells
some minor event, the fulfilment of which
serves as a sign or proof of the future
fulfilment of the whole prophecy; Ex.
—Finally, a wonder, prodigy, miracle,
as a sign of the divine power, i. q. מוֹפֵת,
II. אוֹת or אֹת only c. suff. אוֹתִי, אֹתְךָ,
etc. i. q. אֵת I, pron. demonstr. commonly
as sign of the accus.
אָז demonstr. part. originally of place

line_status.note: The printed word has five letters אורות with a vav (bearing a holem dot) between alef and resh — plene אוֹרוֹת, not defective אֹרוֹת as in Reading B.
Under the tsade a single dot (hiriq) is printed, not a qamets, so A's נִצִּץ is right; but the Arabic is printed with a bare alif (انوار), without the hamza both readings supply.

First word has hataf-patah under aleph and a vav with tsere before resh (אֲוֵרוֹת, the transposed form); second word has qubuts (three diagonal dots) under aleph and qamets under resh (אֻרָיוֹת). Reading A swapped the pointing and dropped the first vav.
Under the first shin of הִתְאוֹשֵׁשׁ the print shows two dots side by side (tsere), not a qamets; Reading B matches. All other characters agree.

Decisive difference is the order of the two forms: the first (leftmost printed) word has its dot above the vav (ḥolem, אוֹת), the word after "or" has the dot mid-height inside the vav (shureq, אוּת). Reading B swaps them.

Between aleph and tav the print has a full vertical vav stroke carrying the holem dot (same plene אוֹ as נֵאוֹת in line 1), not a bare holem over the aleph; so plene יֵאוֹתוּ (B), not defective יֵאֹתוּ (A).

The Conj. III form is printed with two separate alifs (old-style madda), not a single alif-madda as in A; but the hamza+fatha sit on the second alif (the one adjacent to the ta), not on the first as in B, and the comma follows the Arabic directly with no space before it. Hebrew אָתָה and אוֹתָה match both readings.
Printed is אוֹה: the vowel dot sits above the vav (holem, not shureq) and the final letter is he, not tav; Reading A's אוּת is wrong on both. The space before the semicolon is printed.

The nun carries tsere (two horizontal dots), not qamets; the second word begins with a short yod with tsere, not resh, and its holem sits directly over the alef with no vav printed (defective יֵאֹתוּ, contrasting with the plene form on line 2). Reading A is exact.

Under the nun are two horizontal dots (tsere), not qamets, and there is no dagesh in the nun; the second word begins with a short yod pointed tsere (contrast line 1's taller resh/dalet), not resh with hataf qamats. Reading A matches the print.

The middle letter is a broad ת with a top bar and left foot, equal in width to the final ה — not a narrow ו. Context confirms: the defective forms נֵאֹת/יֵאֹתוּ just proposed are being assigned to a root ending in tav (אתה), consistent with the entry preceding "I. אוֹת".

The print shows a holem dot above between א and ו with segol under the ו (אֹוֶת); no qamets is printed under the א, so Reading A's אָוֶת is wrong. Rest of the line is identical in both readings and matches the print.

All three Arabic words carry a clear tanwīn (dammatan, the "G"-shaped mark) above the tāʾ marbūṭa; Reading A omits it. Other points (hamza+fatha on the first, madda on the second) agree with both readings.
After Chald. אָת the printed mark has a dot above a comma tail — a semicolon, not a comma; the rest of the line (qamets under alef, Syriac ܐܳܬܳܐ with zqapha points) is identical in both readings.

Seyame (two dots) is clearly printed, so A is wrong to omit it; but in the image the two dots sit over the waw (the small circle in the middle), not over the first taw as B has it. Zqapha marks on first alaph, waw, and second taw; plain Latin references follow as both readings have.
